entities.summary:
Xiang Xiu (d. 275 CE) was a prominent Chinese philosopher, poet, and scholar of the Cao Wei and early Western Jin dynasties, renowned as one of the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove. His intellectual contributions were pivotal in the development of Xuanxue, or "Profound Learning," a syncretic philosophical movement that reinterpreted classical Daoist and Confucian texts during a period of profound political and social upheaval in 3rd-century China. Xiang Xiu's enduring significance lies primarily in his influential commentary on the *Zhuangzi*, a foundational text of Daoist philosophy, which shaped subsequent interpretations of this complex work for centuries and solidified his place in the intellectual history of the Wei-Jin period.

Emerging from a milieu of intellectual ferment and political instability following the collapse of the Han dynasty, Xiang Xiu joined a circle of unconventional scholars and literati known as the Seven Sages, who retreated to the Bamboo Grove in Shanyang. Though known for their bohemian lifestyle and critiques of officialdom, Xiang Xiu distinguished himself through his scholarly rigor, particularly in his exegesis of the *Zhuangzi*. He undertook the monumental task of providing a comprehensive commentary on the text, completing the first ten chapters before his death. His work aimed to reconcile the seemingly contradictory philosophical stances within the *Zhuangzi*, providing a systematic interpretation that emphasized the concept of "natural spontaneity" (ziran) and the unity of all things.
